title: When honoring is hard
hookLine: many rabbis teach that honor doesn't require accepting harm; distance can be necessary
tomorrow: hands on a kid's head every Friday night. what's being said?

cards: Some family dinners are the kind people post. Some are the kind people brace for in the car on the way over.
The Talmud praises a man named Dama ben Netina, whose mother struck him in front of others, and who didn't shame her back. So does honoring a parent mean taking whatever they hand out?
Two great teachers of Jewish law looked at the hardest case and gave different answers.

teach.h: MAIMONIDES: YOU MAY GO, AND ARRANGE CARE.
teach.b: The case is painful. A parent's mind has become so ill that the child can't care for them without coming apart. Maimonides, in his code of law, says: honor them as far as their state allows.

But if the child can't bear it, he may leave and go, and arrange for others to care for the parent properly. His best case: honor is about the parent being cared for, not about the child being destroyed.
Care can be given by other hands, chosen with love. The Raavad, Rabbi Abraham ben David, writes a short, sharp note beside it: this is not right.

teach.h: THE RAAVAD: WHO WILL WATCH HIM THEN?
teach.b: If he leaves, whom will he leave to watch over him?

teach.h: BOTH KEEP THE PARENT IN VIEW.
teach.b: His best case: nobody hired watches a parent the way a child does, and the hardest people to care for are the ones most easily abandoned. Neither says the parent stops mattering.
They disagree about whose hands the care must pass through.
Some rabbis today apply Maimonides' ruling to children whose parents harm them: distance can keep everyone safer, and honor can travel through others, or simply through not shaming them.

teach.h: IN DANGER? REACH OUT. 988 IN THE US.
teach.b: One thing nobody here argues about: if you're in danger at home, reaching out is right.
Call local emergency help, and in the US you can call or text 988.

how: When honoring a parent is very hard, people can ask a rabbi or a counselor for guidance; Maimonides' ruling (Laws of Rebels 6:10) is a key passage in that conversation, and safety comes first.

games.q: what does “when honoring is hard” mean?
o: a ritual for forgiving a parent after they die
cutting off every tie with a difficult parent
caring for a parent while keeping yourself safe

games.q: two great teachers, one hard case — tap the pairs.
p: may leave and arrange others' care
if he leaves, who will watch him?
call or text in a US crisis

s: Jewish law says honoring a parent means accepting any harm
Maimonides lets a child who can't bear it step away and arrange others' care.
the Raavad disagreed with Maimonides about leaving
his note: if he leaves, whom will he leave to watch him?
in this debate, one side says a hard parent stops mattering
both keep the parent at the center; they argue whose hands give the care.

games.q: your cousin says Maimonides settles it: step away. you lean the other way. what's the Raavad's best case?
o: if the child leaves, who will watch the parent? nobody cares like a child.
children must obey a parent whatever happens, so leaving is forbidden.
Maimonides' code isn't part of Jewish law, so it can be ignored.
games.why: that's the Raavad's note beside Maimonides: whom will he leave to watch him? Maimonides' best case is just as real: care can come through other hands.

practice: Bring to mind one relationship that's hard to honor. In one word, name what you'd wish for it. Name what gets in the way.
Then name one small plan that keeps you safe and still keeps some honor: a shorter visit, a kind text instead of a call, another person in the room.

wordCard.voice: When honoring is hard: the tradition argues it out, and both sides keep the parent in view. Distance can be part of care.

carryVoice: Your line: honor with boundaries. Care can travel through other hands. Day four, held gently.

sources.ref: Mishneh Torah, Laws of Rebels (Mamrim) 6:10, with the Raavad's gloss
